articles.title: White House vs. Microsoft, AI fighter jets, and a visit to a startup founder’s Seattle recording studio
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: This week, we take the GeekWire Podcast to Front Burner Studios in Seattle, where we’re hosted by studio co-owner Seth Paul , who’s co-founder and CEO of security startup Qinsay .

We discuss the White House crackdown on Microsoft’s green-card sponsorships, which Vice President JD Vance announced just hours before President Trump awarded Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. We talk about the contrast, and about how Nadella himself traveled that same path from H-1B visa to U.S. citizenship.
We also look at how Seattle-area startups raised a record $3.5 billion , driven largely by companies building physical things like rockets and satellites.
That leads us to Shield AI’s plans to build AI-piloted fighter jets in Des Moines, Wash., where a city FAQ assures residents the facility is not a data center.
After we catch up on the news, Seth joins us to tells us about the studio, including the vintage console he drove from Detroit, and how he brings a musician’s approach to the startup world.
And in the final segment, it’s the return of the GeekWire Trivia Challenge.
Subscribe to GeekWire in Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you listen.

articles.title: Billionaire Jeff Bezos: ‘Success is not villainy’
articles.author: John Cook
paras: When Jeff Bezos sat down on Blue Origin’s Cape Canaveral factory floor for an interview with Fox News’ Bret Baier earlier this week, he laid out an unapologetic defense of free enterprise and wealth creation.

The Amazon founder’s point was simple: building a massively successful enterprise isn’t something society should apologize for or view with suspicion, it’s the natural result of creating something people actually want.

“There’s nothing wrong with making unbelievably good chicken that people love,” Bezos said, referencing the growth of Raising Cane’s and why restaurant entrepreneurs deserve their wealth. “And it doesn’t make him a bad person.”

Bezos, who stepped down as CEO of Amazon in 2021 and left Seattle for Miami in 2023, is currently the second richest person in the world with an estimated net worth of $380 billion, according to Forbes .

Bezos and Amazon transformed the Seattle region. The company now employs roughly 50,000 corporate and tech workers in the Puget Sound region, divided between its primary headquarters in Seattle and its growing operational footprint in Bellevue.

And his recent comments come at a key moment for Washington state, where voters will decide on Initiative 645 — a high-profile ballot measure aimed at repealing the state’s recently enacted high-earner tax and prohibiting future income taxes.

Bezos, along with other business leaders like former Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz , have claimed that scapegoating wealthy entrepreneurs risks driving away innovation. Bezos argued that politicians targeting business leaders are misdiagnosing the problem, noting that while affordability and social challenges are real, heavy-handed government interventions often fail to solve them.

“If there’s a politician who’s picking villains and pointing fingers, that probably means they don’t have a solution,” Bezos said. He noted that executives who relied on blame-shifting inside his own companies “wouldn’t be in our company for long.”

Watch the full interview below where Bezos also discusses the impact of AI on jobs, the need to beat China in the race to the moon and orbital data centers in space. The portion of the interview where Bezos notes that “success is not villainy” starts in minute 16.

articles.title: New Flyover Video Shows Latest West Seattle Link Design
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Sound Transit has officially reached the 30% design milestone on the West Seattle Link project, celebrating the occasion by releasing a new flyover video that shows renderings of the entire 3.9 mile planned light rail line between SoDo and Alaska Junction. Set to open by 2035 , the 3 Line is the next light rail project planned for construction in the wake of a feverish pace of grand openings over the past two years.

The new images, which reflect the project's design as of this past July, provide an illustration of the significant amount of value engineering that Sound Transit conducted on the line – work that likely saved the project from the chopping block this past spring as the agency grappled with a major budget gap.

From a slimmed-down SoDo station – which will be the northern terminus of the line until the Ballard Link project opens as early as 2042 (or as late as 2060) – to a more compact Alaska Junction, Sound Transit was able to drive down the cost of the line by more than $2 billion between 2024 and 2026.

That work to cut costs has come with real trade-offs for riders. The video shows the new plan for the 3 Line to enter a tunnel near Nucor Steel's West Seattle plant at SW Yancy Street, bypassing a planned station under Avalon Way SW that would have served a growing section of the neighborhood. Without that station, Sound Transit was able to redesign the location of the planned guideway and tunnel portal to avoid having to displace several high profile properties, including a portion of the West Seattle Health Club.

But in contrast with the infill station that opened in North Seattle late last month, it will not be possible to come back later and build Avalon Station down the road if Sound Transit's finances somehow turn around, or voters approve a Sound Transit 4.

On August 13, Sound Transit and the City of Seattle announced another major design refinement for West Seattle Link, one that would be hard to notice in a flyover rendering. A major transmission line that is currently located next to the dedicated busway through SoDo will be relocated closer to the planned light rail guideway, avoiding major disruptions on a nearby street.

"The new SODO segment design will relocate major City infrastructure, Seattle City Light’s 230 kilovolt and 26 kilovolt transmission poles and lines, entirely within the light rail project footprint in the SODO Busway," a City announcement noted at the time. "This means that Sound Transit will not need to move massive powerlines onto 6th Ave S, which significantly reduces construction and lasting impacts on adjacent properties and businesses. The new design is expected to save the project over $100 million and remove the risk of damage to other critical City transportation and water infrastructure."

Since the May 28 board vote that rebalanced the larger Sound Transit 3 (ST3) plan and kept West Seattle Link on track, Sound Transit officials have been touting how swiftly the agency has been moving and heading toward construction. In August, the board unlocked an additional $765 million in budget authorization, setting up a construction support services contract that includes preparations for the Duwamish River crossing.

Just last week, the board's system expansion committee approved another set of property acquisitions, including the West Seattle Corporate Center (the former Bartell Drugs corporate headquarters), which will become a major truck staging point for tunneling work to Alaska Junction. If approved by the full board later this month, that will mark the fifth set of property acquisition approvals that the agency has received, getting the agency's real estate team to work.

This week's flyover video makes work that is often happening behind the scenes more tangible for future riders, even if an opening date nine years in the future seems incredibly distant. Once the 3 Line is fully connected with the rest of the light rail network with the opening of Ballard Link, travelers getting from Westlake Station to Alaska Junction will see their travel times cut by 50%, a major upgrade from current C Line service. But there's a lot standing in the way of that benefit becoming reality.
For now, transit fans will have to live vicariously through YouTube.

articles.title: The Roundup: Why Would We Replace Route 7?
paras: When I was growing up, I had the key to the city.

Anywhere I needed to go, the 7 had my back. I remember when a ride cost less than a dollar. Basketball practice, teen dances at Rainier Vista Boys & Girls Club, Teen Late Night — back when you could run a few games at Rainier Community Center, then hop the 7 and get games in at Rainier Beach.
Then I grew up. My first job was at NikeTown downtown. Guess which bus I used to get there? That's right, the 7.
And it's not just me. The 7 is the second-most-used bus route in King County.

When I learned from Emerald contributor Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero that there were plans on the table to end Route 7 in favor of a RapidRide line in 2032 , I was confused. Who would this serve? Who asked for this?
The proposal would eliminate over 20 stops — in the South End — and would make the bus come less frequently.

My mind goes to the seniors, the students, the workers in our community who are not simply commuting downtown, but using transit to get to places within the neighborhood. How can that happen if 20 stops disappear? Are the elderly or differently abled folks supposed to walk a mile to access a bus stop?
The 7 is more than a bus line; for many in our community, it's a lifeline.

This week, I spoke with Jacquelyn about this proposal. She went on a ride-along on the 7 , with elected officials and community members, to see the stops that would be eliminated and speak with some of the South Enders who would be impacted.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
MD: You've been following this proposal to replace the 7. Can you briefly tell us what has happened and where we are in the process?

JJR: The proposal essentially has the goal of making buses faster and more reliable, and comes from King County's intention to improve bus services overall. So RapidRides are becoming more and more popular in King County. The South Seattle RapidRide line was proposed in 2019 and delayed due to the pandemic. The project picked back up in August. Right now, we're at the phase where King County Metro is presenting it to King County Council. So, essentially, they're going to go to the Council and present what's called an alignment ordinance, and they're briefing the Council on the most updated project that they have. It'll also be an opportunity for community members to go to King County Council and share their thoughts on what they think about the project, and there could potentially be a vote in November about whether King County Council actually fully approves this project or not.
MD: I heard the RapidRide line does two things simultaneously — runs less frequently than the 7 and has 20 less stops. This true? If so, how can Metro call this more efficient?

JJR: Yes. I think that's the question that a lot of community members have. I think that's the big question on whether this project actually makes sense for the South End, and community members certainly don't think so. I think these are part of the concerns that community members and advocacy organizations are bringing up to the Council. Everyone appreciates the investment, but they're not sure it makes sense.
MD: I saw the video of you on this ride-along. Can you tell me who organized it, who attended, and what you learned from community members?

JJR: It was organized by the Nondrivers Alliance and the Transit Riders Union. Community members showed up, like people who ride the bus, leaders from a few community organizations, and a few current and potential politicians. Rebecca Saldaña and Toshiko Hasegawa came; they're candidates for the King County Council seat that represents the South End. Kelabe Tewolde was there; he's running for the 37th Legislative District, the House seat. And then City Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck [was there].

I personally got to see which stops could potentially be eliminated, and I think for people who don't take the bus a lot, it's hard to imagine how long of a distance the potential stops could be. For someone who has a disability or is older, or even a family who has a stroller, walking those longer distances can be really challenging, especially along Rainier Avenue, because there are a lot of infrastructure improvements that need to happen. The sidewalks are uneven, and it can really be hard for a lot of people to navigate.

A lot of what I'm hearing from people is that they're confused about this proposal. It's a very important line, and even aside from the nostalgia aspect, it's the second-most-used bus line in the entire county. Over 11,000 people use it every day. So people were confused about why this was happening.
MD: Why can't we have the RapidRide line and the traditional 7? Why is this an either-or situation?

JJR: That is a question a lot people have for the Executive and the Council. Why can't we have both? A lot of people mentioned the importance of the 7 in terms of navigating Rainier Valley and getting to important places, like grocery stores, pharmacies, and businesses. A lot of people use it in the South End without going downtown.
Budget season is here. Proposals are being presented. And the community is coming out in full force for input.
Developers want to axe a beloved weeping willow tree on South Brandon Street. Neighbors say “No way.” Can we have housing density and trees?
Is the U.S. government complicit in the war in Gaza? On Oct. 10, organizers from around the country will meet in Seattle for a tribunal to determine the answer.
Businesses in Rainier Beach are focused on two things: safety and service.
On Oct. 10, the Emerald will host a forum to introduce the community to the two candidates looking to represent the South End on the King County Council.

This is an abbreviated version of The Roundup newsletter. To get the entire newsletter, including a weekly list of events to check out and my shout-out to South End Gems, subscribe here . See you next week!

Mike Davis is the newsletter editor and Voices editor at the South Seattle Emerald. Born and raised in Seattle's South End, Mike is a longtime journalist who's covered everything from arts and culture to sports to politics.

articles.title: Dear Hendrix
articles.author: Eva Walker
paras: It’s the spooky season. And while I can’t wait to take you out trick-or-treating this Halloween, I wanted to preface the festive occasion with a little music for you (and all those folks reading this on their cell phones at home).

But when your mother is a professional DJ, a playlist can’t just be any old playlist. It has to include a little music education . So here goes! Musically speaking, when most people hear the word “goth,” bands like the Cure, Bauhaus, and Joy Division likely spring to mind. But goth, to me, is something different entirely.

I think of blues artists like Blind Willie Johnson, Son House, and Robert Johnson. These are songwriters and performers that taught me about darkness. They amplified American folklore, singing about figures like John Henry, the folk hero steel driver, the same way others might have heralded Hercules.

So I highlighted five songs by these artists who tell the story of the eerie, haunting American South, from its dark past to its chilling music. These artists, who thrived around the turn of the 20th century used their guitars like hammers, forging timeless masterpieces, despite the backdrop of slavery, the Civil War, lynchings, and extreme poverty. To me, they’re all goth.
P.S. There will be another letter going more into this interpretation of Goth through the lens of black history. But for now, enjoy the tunes.
“Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground” by Blind Willie Johnson (1927)

If the title isn’t goth enough for you already, wait until you give this song a listen. The track is all slide guitar and hums . What I love about these old recordings is feeling like I’m in the same room as the artist. The sound of the slide knocking against the fretboard and the sound of antique silence haunting in the background as Johnson hums is divine. The song displays great loneliness, grief, and heartache. Johnson lost his sight at a young age, when his stepmother threw lye in his face while arguing with his father. Later, in 1945, Johnson’s house was destroyed in a fire, but he stayed there living in the ruins until he died that September. If that isn’t the foundation for some dark music, I don’t know what is.

I’ve loved Son House for as long as I can remember. His song “Death Letter Blues” is goth at its finest. As soon as the track begins, we hear a slide screaming for answers. Son House sings with it, “I got a letter this morning, how do you reckon it read?” As the song continues, we learn the heartbreaking answer. The gal the singer loves is dead . The force behind Son House’s guitar is enough to make you want to get up and dance and holler, which is a strange feeling because he’s delivering to us some pretty awful news. Leave it to the blues to make death this vivacious … Son House is so dynamic, he makes his guitar sound like two people are playing at once—maybe it’s the angel and the devil on his shoulder—one on rhythm and one on lead. Everything sounds delightfully messy on the metal-bodied resonator. There is no wrong note Son House can hit in this song’s story of death and grief.
“Cross Road Blues” by Robert Johnson (1936)

Robert Johnson is likely the most influential blues guitarist to ever live. And his song “Cross Road Blues” is one of his most famous tracks—even now. Like the Son House song, this tune was recorded with just Johnson and his guitar. Although, also like the song above, the artist’s playing can easily be mistaken for two sets of hands. We don’t see the devil or the angel, we just hear them. After all, you can’t talk about Johnson without mentioning the infamous legend. How he went down to the crossroads in Clarksdale, Mississippi, and how he supposedly sold his soul to the devil in exchange for wicked guitar chops. Those chops have gone on to influence countless modern legends, from Keith Richards to Jimmy Page. It all begins on this song. (Fun fact: I played a show in Clarksdale in 2019 with my band, but the devil stood us up!)
“Last Kind Words Blues” by Geeshie Wiley (1930)

There is little known of the life of Geeshie Wiley. We aren’t even sure about her actual birth name (some say her real name may have been Lillie Mae). But while we don’t know much about her personal life, some of her music still lives on and, in many ways, that’s all the info we need. For example, just dive into this haunting track. It tells the story of her father going out to fight in the “German War” (World War I). The singer gives instructions on what to do with his body if he is killed. Geeshie’s haunting guitar, backed by the second guitar played by Elvie Thomas (aka L.V. Thomas), features a lead that mimics the main vocal melody. It establishes the mood, the feeling. It sounds like a cruel morning, cold and yet eerily stoic. You can almost know what it feels like to live in that moment thanks to this recording.
“Freight Train” by Elizabeth Cotten (1904)

We can’t talk about the blues without talking about Cotten-picking. The Venn Diagram of the two (the blues and the picking style) comes to us via the artist Elizabeth Cotten. Her song “Freight Train” is about death (my favorite subject!). It’s a common theme in the blues, but Cotten is no common songwriter or performer. She was left-handed and played a right-handed-stringed guitar upside down, plucking the song’s melody with her thumb and the bass line with her fingers. Her instrumentation was so good, it could easily be mistaken for a child’s lullaby. That is, if you didn’t listen to Cotten’s voice. Her shaky and aged voice told us all about loss and how it feels to her. Years later, Cotten was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame for her foundational playing style—and rightfully so. Discovered by the Seeger family while working as a maid, Cotten won her first Grammy at 90 years old. Indeed, if you ever think it’s too late to start on guitar, Henny, just listen to Elizabeth Cotten. She can wake the dead.

Eva Walker is a writer, a KEXP DJ, one-half of the rock duo The Black Tones, and mom to her baby girl, Hendrix. She also co-wrote the book The Sound of Seattle: 101 Songs That Shaped a City , which was released in 2024. Every month for The Stranger , she writes a letter to Hendrix to share wisdom learned from her experiences—and her mistakes. Read all installments here.

articles.title: One Smart Cookie
articles.author: Meg van Huygen
paras: “I’m actually in trouble with the City because of how honest I am on the socials,” Vince Vu deadpans, feigning concern. We’re seated around a tiny table in the front window of Anh Ơi Bake Shop at Sixth and Jackson, and the unvarnished candor I’ve come to know from his IG stories starts pouring out of him right from the jump. “They were like, ‘Actually, you know, as a Restored cohort member, it’d be really great if you could, like, run your ideas between us first?’”

He breaks character, grinning. “I was like, ‘No! What are you talking about? I’m not gonna do that. I don’t even say anything crazy online, guys.’ I’m just like, ‘Hey, it’s tough out here. Come in! Hello! I am selling sweet treats!’”

Behind the friendly face of this neighborhood baker is a skilled political strategy leader, community activist, and storyteller who knows how to light a fire and call folks to action. And after the sweet treats, that’s kind of the entire point of his shop.

Vu opened Anh Ơi Bake Shop in May 2026 as a place to sell his own Vietnamese-inspired cookies and cakes, as well as those of rotating guest bakers. The concept is a collaborative effort—he devotes a tall wooden shelf apiece to fellow Asian American bakers and their creations.

He snagged the 94-year-old storefront—in the historic former Osami’s Barber Shop space in Seattle’s Nihonmachi (Japantown)—as part of Seattle Restored, a program run through the Seattle Office of Economic Development, the Seattle Good Business Network, and Shunpike. The idea is to rent out and thereby revitalize previously empty retail spaces, then sublet them to new businesses rent-free for six months. He says he actually found the long-empty space himself, then worked with Seattle Restored to secure it via the Seattle Chinatown International District Preservation and Development Authority, aka SCIDpda. Seattle Restored’s participants also receive marketing help, enjoy professional photography of their wares, benefit from a citywide media campaign to help boost them up, and are connected with the property’s owners to negotiate a possible future lease. It’s a bullpen for entrepreneurs to try out their ideas, workshop their products, and tweak their business plans accordingly.

The timing seemed great: Anh Ơi would open just in time for the FIFA World Cup. “And we all know how that went,” Vu quips. Famously, the soccer-fan foot traffic that was promised by the city failed to materialize in the CID. That’s when Vu took matters into his own hands and started telling it like it is—via social media. In late June, he kicked off a reel by telling the camera, “I think the World Cup games in Seattle caused my business to have the worst sales day that it’s ever had.”

The FIFA crash and the viral-ish reel that followed were just the beginning of Anh Ơi’s online media blitz. Today, Vu is harnessing as much marketing reach as the socials can bring him, mostly via reels. These include his takes on popular memes with CID themes inserted, and installments of “The Anh Ơi School of Business,” where he “explain[s] business lessons I learned because I was forced to.” Other times, he’s just telling us that persimmons are in season and to look out for all the delicious pastries about to happen.

Another quirk of the project: Everything in the store is prepackaged. “Yeah, my production isn’t here,” he explains. “I bake my own stuff in SoDo, and I buy the wrapped pastries from the other vendors and then sell them here. I’m just shelves. I’m a grocery store.”

The treats themselves are as fascinating as his business model. Gaze at each shelf in Anh Ơi and read all the different placards with the bios of the bakers and the photos of their faces, and it’s like they’re baking little diary entries for us. On the day I interviewed Vu, baker Cindy Vuong, who operates as Sweet Dream Bakes, had pineapple bun cookies and lotus mooncakes filled with salted egg yolks on her shelf, while Alison Shiu from PãoBāo Bread was selling Portuguese-Chinese snacks like corn focaccia buns dressed with dried shrimp chili oil and sesame cookies loaded with spicy Huang Fei Hong peanuts. (To my chagrin, her char siu chouriço bao had sold out—that’s Portuguese chouriço sausage and char siu, aka Chinese barbecue pork baked inside a crispy-crusted milk bread bun.) La Chinita’s Cocina melds Mexican and Muslim Southeast Asian flavors—among owner Philicia Saephan’s goodies is an ube-s’more brownie topped with beef-gelatin-based halal marshmallows. And Vu himself makes a strawberry corn milk cookie and a fried banana cookie that both go crazy and sell out consistently. These shelves are essentially a personal to-do list for me.

There’s a self-serve cooler case in back for things like durian ice cream and canned cà phê sữa đá. The shop also has room for a coffee/tea cart, where several different pop-uppers—like Muni Cafe, whose menu includes, for example, a matcha latte crowned with a cloud of banana cold foam—have camped out for six-week stints.

When asked how he curates his gallery of bakers, Vu says he began with people he’d met in the farmers market circuit. “I’d popped up at lots of different events, festivals, markets… and you quickly figure out who the competitive vendors are and who the chill ones are, who are very collaborative, very open. When I opened this shop, I called all the chill ones and was like, ‘Hey, I love your stuff. Let’s sell together.’”

Vu also recruits new bakers at farmers markets and other pop-ups, plus he gets new folks coming in with samples all the time. He says he always chats with prospective bakers and makers at length to see if they have matched energy, especially since he enjoys hearing people’s food stories. “What I really love is when someone’s like, ‘Oh, I made this because it reminds me of my mom,’ and I can be like, ‘Oh wow, really? Why? Tell me about your mom.’”

Whatever’s happening inside Anh Ơi on any given day, it’s always hyper-creative, and it’s always about to change. If you eat something you love, you can always check the shelf’s sign and follow the maker online to see where else they sell their stuff. In fact, that’s the whole idea: to be a marketing engine for the superhero pantheon of indie Asian American bakers.

How did Vu cook up such a clever concept? “I’ve been a baker my entire life,” he replies, “like as a subplot. I have a master’s in public policy, and I worked in politics—I worked for Dow [Constantine, former King County Executive]. That’s what brought me to Seattle. And then I worked in tech, and even then, I was baking on the side.

“But when I left tech,” he says, “and you hear this all the time, but tech left me completely spiritually defunct. I felt like I was doing evil. Like, ‘I’m an evildoer. I’m not making the world better.’ And that really bothered me.” He decided to do something not evil for a living instead and took a four-month sabbatical to Vietnam to figure out what that was. “I knew I wanted to do something tactile, with my hands. And I wanted to do something that’s very unapologetically me, which is something Asian American– and community-focused. So I sort of marinated in those ideas.”

From the trip emerged the idea for Anh Ơi. The name is Vietnamese for “hey, you,” specifically when addressing an older male. Per the shop’s website, “it’s a tender little call to someone you care about—a brother, a lover, a friend. It’s playful, it’s warm, it’s how we pull each other close.”

The shop’s concept was nudged along into reality by Vu’s background in government, and his years of tech and marketing experience have proved useful too. “I knew that government policies make it really hard to start any business,” he said, “and especially a food business. So I was like, ‘Let me do it in a way that gets around a lot of that stuff.’” Vu says that, by and large, people don’t know—and the city doesn’t make it easy for them to know—that they can start a food business in such a creative, nonstandard way. He suspects he’s gotten some superfluous attention from county health inspectors for publicly telling folks how it’s done. “It’s so funny,” he says, “because the city has sent so many inspectors here, and like, I worked for the government for 10 years. So like, try me, right? Please try me.

“I always tell people if I ever ran for office,” he says, “I’d be a single-issue politician, and that issue would be: We have to fix our small food business process. Like, people are getting crazy diarrhea from shredded lettuce and finding glass in their frozen bread, or whatever is happening from the big conglomerations. And yet you’re gonna come here over and over to try to pick on my tiny-ass business that hasn’t broken any rules?”

As of press time, Vu’s Seattle Restored tenancy expires October 15. What happens next isn’t totally up to him. “I really want to stay. It depends on Restored—I need their blessing.” Hopefully, he says, once he gets it, he’ll be able to coordinate with SCIDpda and the building’s owners directly going forward.

Vu isn’t shy about his jingoism when it comes to the CID, its rich history, and its scads of very beautiful buildings. When he was applying for the Seattle Restored program, the neighborhood was nonnegotiable for him: “This business makes no sense anywhere but the CID.” As such, he’s frustrated with the city’s lack of investment in the neighborhood. He points to a recent application filed by McDonald’s for the prominent former Bartell Drugs space at Fourth and Jackson. “I’m like, ‘Do you want that to happen to the CID?’ So, I tell my friends, ‘There’s a lot of space available here. The spaces are rough. But we can make them better! We’ll invest in the neighborhood—that’s what we do.’”

It’s a tenuous situation, Vu says, to simultaneously rescue a historic district from both empty storefronts and evil empires. “Honestly, the city should be throwing money at us. There’s great food here. We talk about it like it’s one of the gems of the city. These old buildings are great. Tourists come here—it’s one of their main stops. But the city won’t invest in it, and no one is moving here. Why not? The city could be helping us.”

The challenges of operating a business in the CID aside, Vu’s project sure seems like a success on paper. “I’m the most successful Restored installation they’ve had,” he admits. “I do really well here. But from a revenue perspective, it’s still incredibly difficult… I think the bigger thing I’m trying to highlight is that, hey, I’ve had all these supports, and I have a ton of community help, and I get money from these people. And still, even then, whew. It is rough out here.”

With Seattle rent, permit fees, and other operating costs sharply rising to more comedic and nonsensical heights every year, this city deeply needs more creative, unconventional business-building—especially the food kind. Something needs to change, as soon as possible.

To put a bow on it, Vu concludes: “Let’s challenge what the local food landscape looks like. Right? It doesn’t have to be just solitary genius jerk chefs out here. It can be small people you’ve never heard of, sharing ideas and helping each other make them real. That’s why I do what I do.”

articles.title: ‘There is no secret agenda’: Nara Smith on home-making absolutely everything, raising four kids at 25 – and why she’s definitely not a tradwife
articles.author: Charlotte Edwardes
paras: The model, actor and influencer is known for making her own frozen yoghurt, bubblegum or even toothpaste while dressed in immaculate haute couture. But she insists she is not who the internet thinks she is

Nara Smith is not a tradwife, she wants you to know that. Nor is she an ex-tradwife – pace the New York Times who included her in a feature on how ex-tradwives are as popular a movement now as the tradwives were in the first place. Nor was she peddling a tradwife-adjacent lifestyle choice by marrying at 18, having four children by 24, and devoting hours to cooking and documenting it online. Nor is she Mormon, by the way. Although, yes, her husband, the model and former teen heart‑throb Lucky Blue Smith, was raised Mormon, but we’ll get to that. Nor was she telegraphing subliminal religious messages in her content: “There is no secret agenda.” Nor was she abandoning her biracial heritage by wearing her hair in a sleek little bob. Nor was she leaning into a 1950s housewife archetype – even when dressed in a pink and red polka-dot minidress to batch-cook sourdough.

Smith wants you to scrap everything you think you know about her and start again. She also doesn’t care if you don’t. As with her content: “Those that get it, get it. Those that don’t, don’t. And that’s totally fine. I tell people: ‘If you don’t like my content, I won’t see you scroll past me.’ ‘If you need to block me for your own sanity, please do. I promise I won’t know.’ And if you want to stick around, that is beautiful, I’m grateful, welcome.”

articles.title: ‘I just wasn’t going to give up’: the fight to free the longest-serving political prisoner in the US
articles.author: Adrian Horton
paras: Leonard Peltier was imprisoned for 49 years before his sentence was commuted. A new Netflix documentary exposes the ‘corrupt’ system that allowed it to happen

On 20 January 2025, with 14 minutes remaining in his term as president, Joe Biden commuted the life sentence of Leonard Peltier , after years of pressure to release a figure seen by many as the longest-serving political prisoner in the US. The Indigenous activist, a leader within the American Indian Movement (Aim) and an icon of Native American resistance, served nearly 50 years in prison for allegedly killing two FBI agents during a shootout on the Pine Ridge reservation in South Dakota, in 1975 – killings he has always denied, prosecuted in a railroaded trial widely seen as corrupt.

Outside the Florida prison where Peltier was being held that morning were several of the many activists and lawyers who fought for his release, as well as film-makers David France and Jesse Short Bull. The two directors’ long-gestating documentary on Peltier’s fight for justice was set to premiere just a week later at the Sundance film festival with a very different ending, the octogenarian still awaiting a chance to return home to the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa reservation in North Dakota. That morning, there was “a sinking feeling that it wasn’t going to happen”, France said.

articles.title: ‘Like a drill going into my eye’: why the mystery over Havana syndrome refuses to die
articles.author: Shaun Walker
paras: Dozens of CIA officers have been afflicted by debilitating symptoms over the past decade. Are they the result of ‘mass hysteria’? Or are they from attacks with an energy weapon and, if so, who is responsible? And has there been a cover-up?

Shortly after 1am one night in April 2019, a CIA officer on a work trip to London was jolted awake in his hotel room by the most intense head pain he had ever experienced. His body was soaked with sweat and he felt like his eyes were spinning in their sockets. He manoeuvred his way out of bed, hoping to make it to the bathroom to vomit, but found his sense of balance had deserted him. Eventually, he fell back into a fitful, shallow sleep.

The next day, arriving at the work meeting he had travelled for, the officer found he could not remember the names of colleagues in the room, people he knew well. As the meeting got under way, he could barely follow the discussion. Initially, he chalked it up to a terrible – if rather odd – case of food poisoning. But over subsequent weeks, worrying symptoms persisted: brain fog, loss of balance and increasingly harsh tinnitus.

articles.title: Amélie allowed me to embrace my neurodivergence
articles.author: Lillian Crawford; as told to Olivia Ladanyi
paras: Watching a DVD of the French film alone in my room, I saw for the first time a character who moved through the world like I do

Amélie likes the sound of cracking creme brulee with a teaspoon, plunging her hand into a sack of grain, and turning around in the cinema to watch people’s faces in the dark. I like the smell of books and I love cinema, but I hate the sound of people eating popcorn.

Amélie was not the first neurodivergent-coded woman I’d seen depicted in film. There had been Margot Tenenbaum in The Royal Tenenbaums and Suzy Bishop in Moonrise Kingdom – two Wes Anderson characters in whom I’d recognised myself. But Amélie was the first who was at the centre of the story; she’s the titular character and we see things through her eyes. It was the first time I’d seen a woman on screen move through the world as I did: overstimulated, a bit lonely and afraid of the unknown, comfortable in her own company, with firm likes and dislikes and a powerful sense of social justice.

articles.title: ‘Star Wars’ is crossing over with ‘D&D’ in two upcoming books from Wizards of the Coast
articles.author: Thomas Wilde
paras: Wizards of the Coast plans to revisit the Star Wars universe as its next big cross-company collaboration for Dungeons & Dragons .

On the first day of New York Comic Con 2026, one of the reveals at its big Disney/Lucasfilm panel was the upcoming debut of two new sourcebooks for D&D based on the Star Wars universe, a crossover Wizards first teased at Gen Con in July, as part of D&D ’s previously announced Universes Beyond imprint .

The first book, Star Wars Core Rules , is designed to let players of fifth-edition D&D run games set in the established Star Wars universe. The second, Tyro Squadron: Adventures , contains a full campaign for D&D set during the original Star Wars trilogy, which places players in the role of a secret crew within the Rebellion.
Wizards and Lucasfilm offered no further details, save that more about the new Star Wars D&D books may be revealed at the Star Wars Celebration festival in April 2027.
Star Wars has a long and surprisingly complex history in the tabletop RPG space, beginning with West End Games’ Star Wars: The Roleplaying Game in 1987.

Renton, Wash.-based Wizards of the Coast, a Hasbro subsidiary, took over the Star Wars license in 2000 and released a new game, which used the same d20 system that powered 3rd edition D&D. That version of Star Wars lasted until 2010, when Wizards declined to renew its license.

The most recent Star Wars TTRPG was published by Fantasy Flight Games in 2012 and uses the Narrative Dice System pioneered by the third edition of the Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay game. Fantasy Flight exited the TTRPG business in 2020, but its parent company Asmodee moved the Star Wars license to Edge Studio ( Arkham Horror, Genesys ).

Edge Studio has kept Fantasy Flight’s Star Wars in print, but hasn’t released any new content for it in six years. It reportedly retains the Star Wars license despite the new Universes Beyond books from Wizards.

articles.title: Satellite radar tech startup Kapta Space raises $24M from Bill Gates-backed fund and defense investors
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Kapta Space , a Seattle startup building lower-cost, steerable radar sensors for satellites, has raised $24 million in a Series A funding round to scale production and meet growing demand for defense intelligence contracts.

The investment brings total funding to $30 million, following an initial $5 million seed round led by MetaVC — a metamaterials-focused fund backed by Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and former Microsoft executive Nathan Myhrvold . It also previously received a $1.8 million grant from the Department of Defense.

The deal highlights the ongoing momentum in the Pacific Northwest’s commercial space ecosystem, where a growing cluster of venture-backed startups is building hardware alongside major satellite operations like SpaceX’s Starlink facility in Redmond and Amazon’s Leo constellation program.

Founded in 2023 by CEO Milton Perque and Adam Bily, Kapta uses metamaterials for its proprietary Metamaterial Electronically Scanned Array (MESA) architecture. The tech provides high-resolution, geospatial imagery and ground-target tracking without the extreme cost, power demands, and manufacturing complexity of traditional systems.

Both founders bring deep local expertise to the hardware: Perque and Bily were previously engineering leaders at radar maker Echodyne. Perque’s background also includes stops at Metacept and Intellectual Ventures, while Bily served as an antenna engineer at Apple and satellite startup Astranis.
The fresh capital will help Kapta expand manufacturing, qualify its hardware for spaceflight, and prepare for initial orbital demonstration missions.

Kapta’s software-defined architecture aims to make persistent satellite tracking feasible at constellation scale, letting spacecraft rapidly steer beams to continuously detect and hold custody of moving targets across air, sea and land.

“The mission calls for persistent awareness, and that requires us to rethink how radar has to work at constellation scale,” said Milton Perque, Founder and CEO of Kapta Space, in a release . “Traditional architectures are cost-prohibitive and were never designed for the scale these missions now demand.”

Washington Harbour Partners, which specializes in defense tech investing, led the round, with Bison Ventures co-leading. Previous backer MetaVC Partners joined alongside MYDA Capital, Entrada Ventures, Aurelia Foundry, and Fitz Gate Ventures.

“Kapta’s MESA architecture changes that equation with a modular, highly manufacturable approach to electronically steerable radar,” said Mina Faltas, Founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners. “We believe its combination of performance, cost, and scalability will make Kapta a foundational supplier to the next generation of U.S. and allied space architectures, and we’re thrilled to lead the Series A.”

articles.title: From H-1B to CEO: How Satya Nadella traveled the path the U.S. just cut off for Microsoft workers
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Satya Nadella arrived in the U.S. from India in 1988 to study computer science. Over the next three decades, he went from a temporary work visa to permanent residency to American citizenship, and rose up the ranks at Microsoft to become only the third CEO in its history.
“I don’t think my story would be possible anywhere else,” Nadella wrote in his 2017 book, “Hit Refresh.” “I am proud today to call myself an American citizen.”

On Thursday, President Trump personally handed the Microsoft CEO the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. The award cited his “transformative leadership of a critical American technology company, which led to its rejuvenation for a new era of cloud computing.”

Nadella thanked Trump on X , writing that he was “humbled to stand alongside so many giants of American innovation.” The other honorees were Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, who also received the technology medal; and Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su, who received the National Medal of Science.
Five of the six were born outside the country.

Hours earlier, the Trump administration had suspended Microsoft from the federal program it uses to help foreign workers take the same path to permanent residency. Vice President JD Vance said the company had abused the system by laying off American workers while hiring foreign workers, and called H-1B workers “foreign indentured servants.”
“Our message to Microsoft is you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said at a White House news conference .

Two different programs: The suspension doesn’t stop Microsoft from hiring foreign workers on H-1B visas. Those are temporary work visas, typically granted for three years at a time and generally limited to six years, with some exceptions. They’re overseen by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Amazon is the bigger user of H-1B visas. It received more than 19,000 approvals for H-1B petitions in fiscal 2025, about three times Microsoft’s total, according to an analysis of USCIS data by the National Foundation for American Policy. The totals include renewals and extensions, so they don’t represent individual workers.
The program to which Microsoft lost access comes later in the process.

Known as PERM , it’s run by the Labor Department and is usually the first step when a company sponsors an employee to stay in the U.S. permanently. The employer has to advertise the job and show that no qualified, available U.S. worker can fill it. Most applications are for people already working in the U.S. on H-1B visas.

Microsoft is the biggest user of PERM. The Labor Department ruled on 3,161 of its applications in the fiscal year that ended in September 2025, more than for any other employer in the country, according to a GeekWire analysis of the agency’s data . Microsoft also led in the first nine months of fiscal 2026, with 1,683 applications decided through June.

Amazon and Google filed thousands of PERM applications in 2022 and early 2023, then largely stopped. The Labor Department ruled on 39 applications from Amazon and its subsidiaries last fiscal year, including Whole Foods, Audible and Zappos, and three from Google.

The suspension could hit hardest for Microsoft employees already on H-1B visas. Many count on the company to start the permanent residency process in time to extend their visas past the usual six-year limit, and the Labor Department says it won’t process Microsoft’s pending applications either.

Some Microsoft employees on H-1B visas were surprised by the news and unsure whether it would affect them, The Seattle Times reported . The paper noted that the White House hasn’t provided evidence of fraud by Microsoft.

Microsoft’s response: In a statement posted Thursday , Microsoft pushed back on criticism of its hiring and said it looks forward to “providing the Administration with additional information.” The statement focused on H-1B visas and didn’t address the PERM suspension specifically.

The company said about 80% of the roughly 6,000 H-1B applications it filed last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of people who already work at Microsoft. “These were not to hire new people,” it said.
The rest were for new hires already living in the U.S. legally, a group equal to about 1% of Microsoft’s U.S. workforce. “They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company said.

Microsoft also said it files H-1B petitions only for workers who meet “the rigorous standards of this visa category,” pays them “the same as any other employees doing comparable work,” and offers wages “among the highest of all H-1B filings.”
The vast majority of its U.S. employees are Americans, the company said.

Nadella’s own path: Nadella’s route to citizenship wasn’t a straight line, as he described in “Hit Refresh.” He was working at Microsoft when he married his wife, Anu, in India in December 1992. The next summer, her application for a visa to join him in the U.S. was rejected because she was married to a permanent resident.
Spouses of permanent residents faced long waits, and Microsoft’s immigration lawyer told Nadella it could take five years or more to bring her to the U.S.

Nadella considered quitting Microsoft and moving back to India. Then the lawyer suggested a different approach: give up his permanent residency and go back to a temporary H-1B visa, which would let his wife join him right away.

In June 1994, Nadella went to the U.S. embassy in New Delhi, past the long lines of people hoping to get visas, and told a clerk he wanted to give up his permanent residency. The clerk was dumbfounded, Nadella wrote. The plan worked, and Anu joined him in Seattle, where they started a family. Nadella eventually got back on the path to permanent residency and later became a U.S. citizen.

But in the meantime, back in Redmond, Nadella became known around the Microsoft campus as the guy who gave up his green card. Colleagues called him for advice. One, Kunal Bahl, later left Microsoft when his H-1B ran out before his permanent residency came through. He returned to India and founded the e-commerce company Snapdeal.
“Such is the perverse logic of this immigration law,” Nadella wrote.

articles.title: Microsoft 2.5: GitHub COO Kyle Daigle on stitching the developer universe together
articles.author: Mary Jo Foley
paras: GeekWire is profiling over the next few weeks some of the people and teams that are shaping the evolution of Microsoft in what we’re calling its “Microsoft 2.5” era .

A delicate dance: In August 2025, Microsoft moved to integrate GitHub into the mothership, under its CoreAI division, after having allowed it to run as a quasi-independent entity since acquiring it in 2018. At the same time, GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke announced he would leave the company at the end of the year.

A number of developers feared the worst: GitHub would become just another arm of Microsoft and lose the community-mindedness that had made it attractive to developers of all stripes, and especially open-source ones.

GitHub Chief Operating Officer Kyle Daigle — a 13-plus-year GitHub veteran — had been one of the main champions of the need to “keep GitHub GitHub.” He maintained that stance even after he added the “Chief Marketing Officer of Developer” title for all of Microsoft to his COO role in January 2026.

So, how has Microsoft done this past year with managing GitHub? In an interview with GeekWire , Daigle acknowledged that GitHub’s relationship with Microsoft has changed since the end of the standalone CEO era. But the goal is no longer just “don’t break GitHub.” It’s to export GitHub’s community, developer-first ethos and learnings across Microsoft.

GitHub has influence beyond just the GitHub product set now, Daigle said. And the fact that Microsoft opted to consolidate its developer-facing messaging and community outreach under Daigle, someone who came from GitHub, not from Microsoft’s traditional DevDiv organization, gives weight to his claim.

“Bringing teams together — engineering teams and marketing teams and everyone that wasn’t talking to each other before — has been a really big part of the work,” Daigle said. “I see all these opportunities for GitHub to directly help and impact the overall mission of Microsoft versus keeping it cloistered in a way that isn’t helping either GitHub’s mission or Microsoft’s mission.”

These days, developer teams across Microsoft and GitHub are sharing foundations and the GitHub Copilot software development kit across organizations “in a way that would have seemed improbable before,” he said.
As Microsoft historians know, “Microsoft’s challenge isn’t creating products. It’s connecting them,” Daigle said.

Growing pains: At the same time, the rise of AI agents has strained GitHub’s infrastructure. Over the past few months, GitHub has experienced some significant outages, including one in August that lasted nearly eight hours .

GitHub officials have said they are migrating from their own datacenters to Azure to try to ease some of the capacity issues. Daigle said it’s not a simple lift-and-shift process; rather, it’s a major re-architecture for the platform.
GitHub is roughly 60% through its Azure migration as of early October, he said.

It’s working with Azure storage teams on separating compute and storage for the Git distributed version control system to help alleviate bottlenecks caused by developers and agents working concurrently in the same repositories. Developers and agents made 7.38 billion commits on GitHub in September alone, according to the company.

GitHub’s recent growth would not have been manageable without Microsoft scaling expertise and Azure support, Daigle said. GitHub is in a unique position of being able to request major additional capacity, such as millions of CPUs, and work with Microsoft teams to provision it, he said.

The GitHub app and agent store: GitHub got its start as a platform for source control and collaboration. But its role is evolving as part of its Microsoft integration. In addition to developing and supporting Microsoft’s most successful Copilot, GitHub Copilot, GitHub has an important place in Microsoft’s agent-centric strategy.

GitHub is becoming “the store for anything that needs to be coded and needs some verification,” Daigle said. “We’ll connect you to whatever the right tool inside of Microsoft is for you to run that or whatever tool you’re using, not just (from) the Microsoft product suite.”

In the new world order, GitHub isn’t just the store for apps. Increasingly, it’s also the store for agents, which means GitHub is acting as the developer layer for Microsoft’s “agent factory” strategy.

(Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates envisioned Microsoft as a “software factory” that could produce software at scale. These days, CEO Satya Nadella and team talk about Microsoft as an “ agent factory,” helping customers create agents at scale.)
GitHub currently serves more than 200 million developers, plus an unknown but quickly growing number of agents.

Developers need to be thinking in new ways when it comes to agents, Daigle said. They need to consider ideas such as scaling application programming interfaces (APIs) for agents separately from humans, creating APIs designed specifically for agents, rewriting documentation and tooling so agents can consume GitHub efficiently, and treating agent access as a fundamentally different workload from human access.

In the longer term, Daigle said he expects AI to make software economically viable for smaller audiences, such as a family, an individual or a single team. The app-store model may change substantially in the coming years, as people create highly specialized applications. GitHub could help like-minded users discover software for specific interests, such as a narrowly focused household or community use case.

GitHub historically has considered anyone who has seen or touched code to be part of the developer community. Daigle’s vision is for GitHub and Microsoft to let both professional developers and newer builders create and run software and agents without needing to manage token costs, uptime, monitoring or operational overhead.

GitHub will have more to say about its plans at the GitHub Universe conference in San Francisco, Oct. 28-29. The event won’t focus on code generation alone; it will include information on tools covering the full lifecycle, proactive security approaches and how to determine whether software is working well after deployment.

“We’re looking to solve the core parts of the platform, like Git, like Actions, in a way that I hope will make people excited and feel like they can absolutely trust GitHub for the next decade to come,” Daigle said.

articles.title: Tug-of-War Over New Transportation Funding Heats Up in Bellevue
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Bellevue City Council is on the cusp of approving a pair of new funding sources to bolster transportation infrastructure later this fall, but the fight over what exactly those new dollars should fund is far from settled. The debate playing out now is set to decide which transportation projects the Eastside's largest city prioritizes over the next decade, as it prepares to accommodate significant housing growth around public transit.

This week city officials formally presented a set of scenarios that outlined how Bellevue would use projected revenue from a potential 0.1% increase in the city's sales tax rate as well as a $20 car tab fee, unlocked from a transportation benefit district that the city has been considering tapping into since 2023. The sales tax bump would be expected to generate around $100 million for transportation infrastructure over 10 years, with the car tab only bringing in $20 million over the same period.

Sustainable transportation advocates in Bellevue have been pushing for a major infusion of resources to help reduce deaths and serious injuries, and that push has been backed up by a bloc of councilmembers standing behind the idea of prioritizing safety investments. But many of Bellevue's business interests are pushing for more investments in "underperforming" intersections to make it easier to drive around the city.

If the Council decides to adopt both the sales tax hike and the car tab next month, Bellevue would be poised to invest an additional $35 million over a decade in bike and pedestrian improvement projects, as well as $16.4 million more in neighborhood traffic calming. Combined, those two categories would amount to 41% of the city's total transportation spending, roughly aligning with levels proposed by Bellevue Transportation Director Andrew Singelakis during an initial budget discussion this spring.

The "major projects" category would amount to a full 35% of spending and 33% of new dollars, with the majority of that new spending devoted to completing the next phase of Spring Boulevard (Zone 3) through the BelRed neighborhood. Framed as a multimodal project, the $74.8 million connection would create an alternative for pedestrian-hostile Bel-Red Road – which the Council decided against making safer for people on bikes in 2024 . But with two general purpose lanes beefing up the need for property acquisition, the benefits of the project for people who walk and bike in Bellevue won't really align with its cost.
There's also the fact that the road cuts right through what is intended to be a new park for the future residents of BelRed.

The scenarios laid out on Tuesday do invest plenty in vehicle capacity in their own right. Scenario two, which includes only the sales tax increase, includes $18.9 million in new funding for projects specifically intended to address driver travel times on top of $49.3 million under the status quo. That includes $10 million to widen two intersections to improve traffic flow. With scenario three, which includes the new car tab fee, that would increase to $25 million, getting another intersection widening across the finish line.

There's also the issue of the Grand Connection Crossing , Bellevue's plan to build a pedestrian bridge over I-405 between Downtown and Wilburton and create a brand new multimodal connection as well as an opportunity for placemaking. Under either scenario 2 or 3, the $265 million project would receive a $10 million investment, freeing up dollars that had been set to go to the crossing from the general fund – dollars that could potentially go to any other city spending. Recently the City of Bellevue received buy-in from several regional governments to tap into tax-increment financing to pay for a much bigger share of that project's total cost.

These potential funding sources recently won over a major Bellevue stakeholder. Three years ago, the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce had initially opposed the idea of tapping into the unutilized transportation benefit district, which cities like Seattle have long been using to fund infrastructure. But now they've come around, officially conveying support for the move Tuesday night. But the business group, which has convened a Bellevue Mobility Coalition to weigh in on transportation issues, has conditions.

The group has framed an intense desire to see the sales tax revenue generated by the 0.1% increase – "paid largely by businesses" – serve the city's high-growth areas like Downtown, Wilburton, Factoria, and Eastgate. The smaller tranche of car tab funding, the group said in an October 6 letter, should "primarily benefit neighborhoods."

In comments Tuesday night, a Chamber representative also told councilmembers they want to see any additional funding that comes in beyond projections get devoted to vehicle infrastructure – namely intersections that are considered "deficient" in terms of how much delay drivers experience getting through them. The group also made clear that they don't support the idea of repurposing traffic lanes to create bicycle facilities, one of the most cost-effective ways for cities to make streets safer.

"Our support depends on four things. First, funding for Spring Boulevard Zone 3, 120th Avenue NE Stage 4, and the Grand Connection stays sufficient to complete the projects," Tony Sprague, Public Policy Manager for the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce, told councilmembers. "Second, the underperforming intersections fund is increased and focused on growth corridor arterials with the first $10 million of any surplus sales tax collections dedicated. Third, vehicular capacity is not reduced for bicycle facilities except as a last resort. Fourth, sales tax revenue is not shifted to neighborhood programs that the car tab should fund."

Mariya Frost, Vice President of Government Affairs for Kemper Development Company (a member of the Bellevue Mobility Coalition), went even further than the Chamber, requesting that the Council put the revenue sources to a public vote and suggesting the proposals invest too much in walking and biking. The company, which recently announced an intention to sell its holdings in Bellevue, has been actively involved in transportation decisions in the city going back decades.

"If council decides to move forward without a public vote, project funding must prioritize traffic congestion relief and accommodating vehicular travel associated with Bellevue's growth," Frost said. "The rationale I've heard is that we need to balance the system across all modes, but it makes little sense to disproportionately pour millions of dollars into lower demand infrastructure while the roadway network carrying nearly 70% of our workers and residents is actively breaking down."
But so far Councilmember Jared Nieuwenhuis has been the lone voice on council framing either scenario as investing too much in walking and biking.

"Throughout the different scenarios, there's substantially more funding for bikes and pedestrians than vehicles," Nieuwenhuis said. "You're looking for that balanced approach, [a] multimodal approach. I totally agree with that, but I'm also cognizant of the fact the vast majority of people that who come into our city do so in a vehicle, in their car."

Other councilmembers have only expressed frustration that the investments the city has planned aren't able to be implemented sooner, but also haven't signaled a willingness to rebalance any of the funding scenarios by prioritizing safety projects over intersection widenings.

"Every year at this time, we have the Walk and Roll to School Day commitment proclamation. And I always think to myself, is it really safe to expect that our families are going to ask their kids to walk or roll to school?," Councilmember Lynne Robinson said. "And I know every year it gets a little safer, but we have so many holes in our infrastructure that most families I don't think do feel comfortable having their kids get to school independently, and that just creates a huge line of cars and congestion in our neighborhoods."
Councilmember Naren Briar made similar remarks, echoing comments she made back in April about wanting to see more funding devoted to neighborhood traffic calming and safety upgrades.

"If a seven-year-old has no sidewalks or a crosswalk to rely on when waiting for the bus in the dark at 7am, those children are our top concern for me, and their safety and their well-being, as opposed to prioritizing one mode over the other," Briar said. "I think neighborhood improvement is what I would really like to see. I understand that if we get to a place where taxes have to be raised, I do firmly believe that it needs to prevail through the scenario that benefits the neighborhoods the most."

While the attempt to strike a "balanced approach" illustrates Bellevue's current state as formerly car-oriented suburb trying to find a path toward being a more cosmopolitan place, there are signs that the reality of trying to keep planning around cars is starting to sink in.

"As we grow over the next 20 years, there will be limited capacity for additional vehicle facilities," Deputy Transportation Director Mark Poch said. "Right of way is limited. We have really good regional transportation we need to connect to, a lot of people connect to that by foot or by bike, as you know. Trying to find that balance so that we're able to meet that growth is really the key objective and making sure that we were aligned with what the community thinks – not one for one, but in the same ballpark, I think was important."
Bellevue's budget deliberations are set to continue throughout this month, with major decisions coming at November 3 and 10 meetings ahead of a final vote on November 17.
This story has been corrected to clarify the percentage of total spending set to go to pedestrian & bicycle and neighborhood traffic calming.

articles.title: At Capitol Hill Station, Cha Chak changes the balance on Thai tea
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: $5 A MONTH TO HELP KEEP CHS PAYWALL-FREE Subscribe to CHS to help hire writers and photographers to cover the neighborhood. CHS is a pay what you can community news site with no required sign-in or paywall. To stay that way, we need you. Become a subscriber to help us cover the neighborhood for $5 a month -- or choose your level of support Behind the Cha Chak counter above Capitol Hill Station , making tea looks a lot like pulling espresso.

Servers pour hot tea back and forth between two metal pitchers held wide apart, repeating the motion until the liquid turns frothy and smooth. It is cha chak, the hand-pulled tea style common in southern Thailand and Malaysia. Owner Montida Lertkiatsakul compares the process to steaming milk for a latte. It is not about the dairy, she explains, but about working air into the liquid to create texture.
That aeration carries a brew designed to taste fundamentally different from syrupy takeout versions.
“Usually the Thai iced tea tends to have a lot of milk taste,” Lertkiatsakul said.

Cha Chak blends several strong black teas to keep the flavor bold and significantly less sweet, finishing with a slight bitterness. The green tea skips matcha powder for a green tea base scented with jasmine. Coconut milk is available as a dairy alternative, along with caffeine-free options.

The shop sits on the plaza across from Glo’s Diner , taking over the space left empty where a chain juice bar closed in 2024. It is Lertkiatsakul’s second business on the Hill, coming a decade after she helped opened Manao Thai Street Eats at 14th and Pine. She partnered with Suphanita Roumsak on the new project.
“It’s a good location and a good community,” Lertkiatsakul said.

Desserts share the menu with the tea. Cha Chak serves Thai tea chiffon cake, green tea ice cream lattes, and scoops of mango, chai, and green tea ice cream. A mango sticky rice sundae is also on offer, made with a house mango sauce during the months outside the brief spring window when fresh Thai mangoes are in season.

For visitors, the draw is a rare look at traditional Southeast Asian tea mechanics paired with a menu built from scratch. Between the live theater of hand-pulled brewing, an intentionally bold, less-sugary tea profile, and house-made sweets like the mango sticky rice sundaes and tea chiffon cakes, Cha Chak gives the station plaza a distinct craft alternative.
Find Cha Chak at 118 Broadway E above the plaza along E Barbara Bailey Way. Learn more at chachakseattle.com .

articles.title: Shelf Life
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: As he leads me on a tour of Scarecrow Video, longtime buyer Mark Steiner spots former employee Xoe Amer in the new releases section and waves. Steiner, who started working at Scarecrow in 1992 and retired in September, has worked with Amer’s mom, witnessed Xoe grow up, and seen her work at Scarecrow’s erstwhile coffee stand VHSpresso.

“Just seeing Xoe browsing the shelves, that’s second-generation right there. Right behind the counter, too,” he says, gesturing toward Sophia Soriano, an employee whose mother, Rebecca Soriano, cofounded Scarecrow in 1988. “It blows my mind. We’ve endured, no matter what got thrown at us, and it boggles my mind that we’re still here.”

This kind of relationship is emblematic of Steiner’s 34-year stint at Scarecrow, which has surpassed the entirety of Blockbuster’s 29-year corporate retail era in the US; international stores closed in 2020. He has seen the store go from around 1,000 titles to over 156,000, and nearly every single one has passed through his hands. Even he still sometimes gets overwhelmed by Scarecrow’s massive inventory. “Every day I do my job, and I leave and I have 50 things to watch,” he says. “So I always tell people, ‘I get intimidated in this place too, and I’ve been here.’” As he points out, nobody will live long enough to see every movie in the store.

Steiner may well be the longest-tenured video store employee in history, but you wouldn’t know it from his affable, modest demeanor. “I just put my head down and came to work,” he says. “And the other corollary that is equally important is that it’s a really cool place to work, and everybody who’s run it has always been nothing but supportive.” In 2006, a tree fell on his house, nearly killing both of his children, and Scarecrow bolstered him through the crisis. They also allowed him to work four days a week, enabling him to spend more time raising his kids.

Steiner lights up when he talks about film, gesticulating and reciting a steady stream of trivia from the annals of his cinematic knowledge. As a child in Detroit, he learned to read by poring over film critic Leonard Maltin’s annual movie guide. While home sick with chickenpox one day, he was wowed by North by Northwest on TV. The summer he turned 10, he rode his bike to the theater to see Star Wars , which he says “blew up my world.” His family got a VCR when he was 11, and each of them got to pick out a movie. Steiner chose Robert Altman’s M*A*S*H because he liked the TV series, which was based on the film, and watched it daily. Altman eventually became his favorite director, and some 40 years later, he’d let M*A*S*H actor Tom Skerritt into Scarecrow and chat with him.

At 13, his bubbe took him to see Raging Bull , his first R-rated movie. “That was the first movie that really knocked my socks off that I saw in the theater,” he remembers. Around the same time, his cousin, who worked at a record store in Detroit, introduced him to artists like Mott the Hoople, Lou Reed, and David Bowie, sparking a lifelong love of music and “rabid” record collecting habit. “I’m an omnivore, I guess,” he says. “I like what I like, but I always want more.”

At Michigan State University, Steiner and a friend launched a film club, screening mostly foreign films on campus. He also frequented the Lansing video store Video to Go, which stocked a wide variety of titles and which he calls an “early model” for Scarecrow. After graduation, he moved to Seattle, having absorbed romantic visions of the Pacific Northwest from the films McCabe & Mrs. Miller and Trouble in Mind and the Tom Robbins novel Jitterbug Perfume . There, he became a regular at Scarecrow Video’s original Latona Avenue location. One day in 1992, he walked in feeling completely burned out from working in social services, and the staff encouraged him to apply for a job. Although he accidentally missed a meeting on his first day, the team embraced him warmly, and thus began a decades-long career. The following year, Scarecrow moved to its current Roosevelt location, and the buyer position was created for Steiner.

Steiner’s life is inextricable from his vocation. Even his 1998 wedding vows came from the 1945 romantic drama The Clock , directed by one of his favorite directors, Vincente Minnelli. In the film, Judy Garland (who would later marry Minnelli) and Robert Walker play a young couple who wed within the course of a 24-hour whirlwind romance. Similarly, Steiner and his now-wife fell in love during a 24-hour first date, so the lines felt apt. “We were like, okay, good enough for Judy Garland and Vincente Minnelli,” he says.

His curiosity and humility have served him well, helping him discover titles beyond his own taste. He credits his kids with broadening his horizons and stresses the importance of “know[ing] you’re a dumbass.” “You gotta pay attention, you gotta hear from people, because if it was just me, it’d be all Westerns on the main floor,” he says. “With any curating, I think you can view it with your knowledge, but that shouldn’t be the beginning or the end.”

From his office on the second floor, Steiner could overhear customers talking to staff, which helped him gauge demand and learn about films he wouldn’t have otherwise. No day as a buyer was exactly the same as another. The position demanded grit, adaptability, persistence, and an ability to build relationships with distributors. “It’s a mix of listening to people and just being really, really diligent and detail-oriented, and that’s sometimes a slog,” Steiner says.

Scarecrow almost went out of business in 2014 due to competition from streaming services; Steiner helped them survive as they became a nonprofit and introduced their popular DVD-by-mail program across the country in 2021. “He’s been a stabilizing force through all of that stuff. He’s paid his dues, he’s earned some rest,” veteran employee Joel Fisher says.

Fisher, who helped spearhead Scarecrow’s transition into a nonprofit, is taking over as buyer. He says that the connections Steiner has cultivated with distributors will be the most difficult thing to replace. “That’s going to be a thing that I just have to earn through time and build from scratch. I’ll probably do things in my way and just try to figure out a good way to move forward,” Fisher says. “Things are always changing in this realm. We’re actually in a really good place now that the pendulum has swung back towards people understanding the importance of physical media.”

Fisher will miss Steiner’s dedication. “Mark’s been around forever, so he remembers everything that happens, and he’s really passionate about helping people out,” he says. “He’s dealt with all the special orders and availability checks, so he’ll go out of his way if people are searching for a thing. If he can find it, then he’ll leave no stone unturned, and he’s always really good with that.” Once, Steiner tracked down a VHS copy of Apocalypse Now for an older woman who wanted to watch it because it was her late husband’s favorite film—at the time, DVDs could not be easily paused with the intent of resuming later in the same spot, and she couldn’t sit through a three-hour movie. The year Napoleon Dynamite came out, Steiner went to Costco to buy up their stock because of the extreme demand for it around Christmas, and it was so popular that people were begging to buy copies in the Scarecrow parking lot when he returned.

Steiner has a gold mine of stories about brushes with celebrities and film industry behemoths. He’s seen stars like Bridget Fonda, Roger Ebert, Alejandro Jodorowsky, and Quentin Tarantino (a former video store employee himself) walk through Scarecrow’s doors. When legendary director Bertrand Tavernier came to SIFF in 1997 to promote his film Capitaine Conan , Steiner invited him to the store and followed him around for three hours as he rifled through titles and remarked on them in a thick French accent. He once sat in on director Werner Herzog, actor Crispin Glover, and former Scarecrow employee Norm Hill recording the commentary for Herzog’s film Even Dwarfs Started Small , in which Herzog uttered the sage wisdom, “Chickens are something that frighten me because they are so stupid… When you really take a close look into the eyes of a chicken, it’s really, really weird.”

Kurt Cobain and Courtney Love used to patronize the Latona location. Once, late Scarecrow cofounder George Latsios, who would read back customers’ first and last names in order to memorize them, loudly repeated “Kurt Cobain” several times, having never heard of the Nirvana frontman. “He was trying to keep a low profile, and George is like, ‘Hello, Kurt Cobain! Oh, you’re Kurt Cobain,’ and you see these people in the store, their ears perking up,” Steiner recalls. Still oblivious, Latsios inquired what Cobain did for a living and asked, “You aren’t one of those grunge musicians, are you?” When Cobain responded that he was, Latsios earnestly wished him luck. (For context, this was a week after Nirvana appeared on Saturday Night Live .)

As for Love, she favored British dramas like Brideshead Revisited due to her time living in the UK and would rent a “shitload of tapes” at a time, until Love and Cobain’s nannies inevitably returned them late. She incurred so many late fees that her accountant had to have a talk with her, according to Rebecca Soriano, but Steiner calls it a “wonderfully symbiotic relationship,” since her fines helped support the store.

He’s invigorated by the new wave of younger generations’ enthusiasm for film. “We’re really engaging more and more with customers, and that’s what I’m most excited about,” he says. “It used to be this boys’ club.” He’s seen a rise in interest in body horror, such as Coralie Fargeat’s The Substance , David Cronenberg’s films, and Louise Weard’s Castration Movie series, which sold a staggering 30 copies.

It’s important to Steiner that Scarecrow persists as an archive. He says many people don’t realize that they don’t sell off anything from their stock, unless they’re upgrading existing titles. “If you came in here as a kid and saw something, it should still be here for you 30 years later,” he says. Of Scarecrow’s 100 rarest titles, 88 aren’t even in the Library of Congress.

In retirement, Steiner looks forward to spending time with his wife and his dog Gracie and continuing to pursue his twin passions of movies and music. He’s excited about the possibility of working with Rebecca, who is retiring from teaching third grade, to bring film education to classrooms. Since 2019, he’s also hosted a radio show called Soundtrack Cinema from 7–8 p.m. each Thursday on SPACE 101.1 FM. “I’ve just always wanted to share cool things, and radio is perfect for that,” he says. Every week, he creates a themed soundtrack, using film and TV scores, needle drops, and other film-related music.

Nevertheless, he’ll still be found roaming the shelves of Scarecrow from time to time. “I mean, how could I not?” he says. “I’ve had this at my fingertips for my whole adult life, so I couldn’t conceive of not taking something home when I come in.”
